_metadata.source: World Economic Forum. 'The Future of Jobs Report 2025.' January 2025.
_metadata.surveyBase: Future of Jobs Survey 2024: 1,043 unique employer responses representing more than 14.1 million employees across 55 economies and 22 industry clusters. Respondents are Chief People, Learning, Strategy, and Executive Officers at firms with 500 or more employees; small enterprises and the informal sector are out of scope.
_metadata.fieldwork: Qualtrics, May to September 2024 (p. 97); the metrics appendix says May to August 2024 (p. 99).
_metadata.refreshNote: Figures are employer expectations for 2025–2030 collected in mid-2024. Replace on arrival of the next edition.
_metadata.dataSource: International Labour Organization, ILOSTAT; World Economic Forum Global Skills Taxonomy.

technologyTrends.description: Share of employers surveyed that identify the stated technology trend as likely to drive business transformation.
technologyTrends.keyFinding: AI and information processing technologies are expected to have the biggest impact, with 86% of respondents expecting these technologies to transform their business by 2030.

skillsOnTheRise.description: Skills ranked by net increase — the difference between the share of employers that consider a skill to be increasing vs. decreasing in use, 2025–2030.

coreSkills2025.description: Share of employers who consider the stated skills to be core skills for their workforce in 2025.
coreSkills2025.note: Analytical thinking remains the most sought-after core skill, with seven out of 10 companies considering it essential.

coreSkills2030.method: Skills plotted by 2025 core share (Figure 3.3) against 2030 net increase (Figure 3.4); quadrants split at the median of each axis.
coreSkills2030.description: Core-in-2030 skills are core now and expected to rise; emerging skills rise fast but are not yet core; steady skills are core now without expected increase.

skillGapGrowingVsDeclining._note: Figure 3.7 prints an index (1 = equal requirement) on two O*NET-derived axes; the text extraction carries no per-skill values, so only the ranked findings are recorded.

metrics.importanceGap: how much more essential a skill is for growing jobs
metrics.proficiencyGap: how much more expertise growing jobs require

findings: Resilience, flexibility and agility is the strongest differentiator on both axes.
Programming scores higher on importance but needs less proficiency than technological literacy.
Resource management and operations, and quality control, show marked gaps on both axes.
Analytical thinking is fifth on importance gap and sixth on proficiency gap.
Manual dexterity differs on proficiency, not importance.
Service orientation and customer service is the only skill growing jobs need no more than declining jobs.

skillInstability.seriesNote: Figure 3.1 values are mean employer estimates per survey year: 2016 35%, 2018 42%, 2020 57%, 2023 44%, 2025 39%.
skillInstability.description: On average, workers can expect that 39% of their existing skill sets will be transformed or become outdated over the 2025–2030 period, down from 44% in 2023 and 57% in 2020.

globalEmploymentChange.description: 170 million jobs projected to be created, 92 million displaced, constituting 22% structural churn of the 1.2 billion formal jobs in the dataset, amounting to a net 7% increase.

fastestGrowingRoles._note: Net growth percentages are chart-only data in the source (bar chart without labeled values). Manual extraction from the visual would be needed to populate netGrowthPct fields.

roles.role: Light Truck or Delivery Services Drivers

fastestDecliningRoles._note: Net decline percentages are chart-only data in the source. See fastestGrowingRoles._note.
fastestDecliningRoles._verified: Order confirmed against Figure 2.2 (p. 19) and the Figure 2.3 tail (p. 21).

roles.role: Door-To-Door Sales Workers, News and Street Vendors, and Related Workers

transformationBarriers.description: Share of employers surveyed expecting the stated barrier will hinder their organizational transformation, 2025–2030.

barriers.barrier: Skills gaps in the labour market
Organizational culture and resistance to change
Inability to attract talent to the industry
Lack of adequate data and technical infrastructure
Inability to attract talent to my firm

keyFindings: Skills gaps rank first in 52 out of 55 economies and 19 out of 22 sectors.
This is more pronounced than the 2023 edition, where skills gaps were backed by 60% of executives.

aiAdoptionBarriers.survey: World Economic Forum Executive Opinion Survey, more than 11,000 executives (distinct from the Future of Jobs Survey)

barriers.barrier: Lack of skills to support adoption
Lack of vision among the managers and leaders
High costs of available AI products and services
Lack of customization to local business needs
Complex and costly regulations around the use of AI and data

aiAdoptionBarriers.keyFinding: A persistent gap in skills required for AI adoption, both for managers and workers (p. 62).

generalStrategies.description: Share of employers surveyed planning to implement the stated workforce strategy in response to macrotrends, 2025–2030.

strategies.strategy: Accelerate the automation of processes and tasks
Hire staff with new skills to meet emerging business needs
Complement and augment workforce with new technologies
Transition existing staff from declining to growing roles
Reduce staff whose skills are becoming less relevant or where roles are no longer needed
Move operations within closer control through re-shoring, near-shoring or friend-shoring

aiSpecificStrategies.description: Share of employers planning to implement the stated strategy in response to AI's increasing capability and prevalence.

strategies.strategy: Reskilling and upskilling existing workforce to better work alongside AI
Hiring new people with skills to design AI tools and enhancements
Hiring new people with skills to better work alongside AI
Re-orienting organization to target new business opportunities created by AI
Transitioning people from jobs that AI will cause to decline
Downsizing workforce where AI can replicate people's work
Organization has low exposure to AI

aiSpecificStrategies.keyFinding: Reskilling and upskilling the existing workforce is the top AI-specific workforce strategy, planned by 77% of employers across 45 of 55 economies.

trainingNeeds.accessNote: The 11-in-100 share unlikely to receive training is roughly uniform across industries and geographies (p. 47).
trainingNeeds.description: If the world's workforce was made up of 100 people, 59 would need training by 2030. Of these, 29 could be upskilled in their current roles, 19 redeployed, and 11 would be unlikely to receive the needed reskilling.

industryDeltas2023to2025._note: Professional Services has 2025 data only (Figure 3.8 note).

outcomes.outcome: Transitioning existing employees to new jobs or evolving roles
Increasing talent mobility across different roles
Enhancing reputation and branding of the company
Increasing talent mobility across different geographies

expectedOutcomes._note: Employer expectations of outcomes, not measured outcomes.

reductionAttribution.description: Of the roughly 15-point fall in the human-only task share by 2030, 81.5% is attributed to automation and 19% to human-machine collaboration.

humanMachineFrontier.caveat: Compares 2025 and 2030 proportions only; does not measure change in the absolute volume of work (p. 27).
humanMachineFrontier.description: The proportional share of tasks performed solely by humans is expected to decline from 47% to 33% by 2030, while technology-performed tasks rise from 22% to 34%.

aiSkillDemandByIndustry.note: Share of employers reporting increasing need for AI and big data skills by 2030, by industry.

genAISubstitution.method: Indeed Hiring Lab: GPT-4o rated its own capacity to substitute for more than 2,800 granular skills on theoretical knowledge, problem-solving, and need for physical presence; five levels from very low to very high (August 2024).
genAISubstitution._caveat: Model self-assessment, not observed performance. Figure B3.1 bar values are not in the note extraction.
highestSubstitution: AI and big data (data mining, machine learning applications)
genAISubstitution.employerImplication: Training should focus on advanced prompt-writing skills and broader GenAI literacy (p. 44).

economyProfiles._source: Economy profiles, pages as listed per row; global row from the report's global figures
economyProfiles._fieldDefinitions: AI exposure = share of employers not reporting low AI exposure (User Guide, p. 109). AI transform expected = share naming AI and information processing as a transformation driver (Figure 1.2 question). Human-machine 2030 = share of task time expected to be delivered by humans, both, and technology (p. 110).

profiles.name: Canada
profiles._note: Figure 3.2 (p. 34) prints Canada skill disruption as 38%; the profile prints 37%.

industryProfiles._source: Industry profiles, pages as listed per row
industryProfiles._note: Field definitions and the global comparison row: see economyProfiles.

investmentContext.finding: Since the release of ChatGPT in November 2022, investment flows into AI have increased nearly eightfold.
investmentContext.genAIAdoption: GenAI considerably reduces barriers to usage and the need for specialized technical knowledge through natural language processing.
